blanks.note: BOL record 321 (BCB's own CV, https://www.bcb.gob.bo/webdocs/Gerentes/jvalencia_g.pdf) re-read in full: the only financial employers it names are Banco de la Union S.A. (already settled as state, 97% government-held), Banco de Cochabamba / Banco de Cochabamba S.A., and Compania Boliviana de Seguros S.A.; the rest (Grupo Empresarial Monterrey, Ferrocarril Nuevo Central Argentino, Ingenio Sucroalcoholero Aguai, Jindal Steel Bolivia S.A., Ferroviaria Oriental S.A., Comision Nacional de Estudio de la Cana y del Azucar) are railways, a steel mill, a sugar mill and a state commission, i.e. not private finance at all, so only two employers can ever convert Bolivia. ASFI Libro_Historia_Tomo_II.pdf read at offset 100,000-200,000 (the 1993-1994 banking-crisis chapter): it names Banco de Cochabamba exactly twice, both about its 1994 liquidation - 'En el caso del Banco de Cochabamba, la liquidacion se debio a la no adecuacion de su patrimonio a la Ley de 1993' and 'la liquidacion en 1994 de: BancoSur y Banco de Cochabamba' - and states nothing about who owned it; 'Compania Boliviana de Seguros' does not appear anywhere in that window, which refers only to generic 'entidades aseguradoras'; the window carries no list of 'bancos privados' and cites ASOBAN only as a footnote source. This is the chapter where an ownership statement would have sat, so the document's most likely section is now read and names none.

Two Bolivian candidates refused on the stated-ownership rule. (1) Decreto Supremo 2068 of 30 July 2014 (https://www.bcb.gob.bo/webdocs/normativa/2014%20-%20DS%202068%20-%20Condiciones%20Cierre%20Bancos%20Sur%20y%20otros.pdf) downloaded and grepped in full: it names 'Banco Cochabamba S.A.' in its subject and object clauses and says the liquidator 'continuara los juicios penales instaurados contra los accionistas, ex-directivos' - the existence of shareholders being prosecuted is not a statement that the shareholders were private, and the decree says nothing about who they were. (2) Lexivox's consolidated page for the liquidation decrees (https://www.lexivox.org/norms/BO-DS-23881.html) extracted and searched: it names Banco Sur S.A., Banco de Cochabamba S.A. and Banco Internacional de Desarrollo S.A. only as entities whose liquidation was being closed, with no ownership words. Both are company-law form and silence, which the brief rules out.

ASFI's live registers of banks and of insurers were never opened this round, and remain the fetch that would settle Banco de Cochabamba S.A. and Compania Boliviana de Seguros S.A. at once. Note for the next round: www.asfi.gob.bo and asfi.gob.bo refuse curl outright from this environment - every path tried, including ones a WebSearch had just returned as live (Libro_Historia_Tomo_II.pdf, Historia_de_la_Supervision-tomo-II1.pdf, MEMORIA_1998.pdf), returned an identical 404 HTML page of 83,832 bytes, while WebFetch served the same Tomo II file normally. So ASFI must be worked through WebFetch, which means the grep-the-PDF method is unavailable there and each ASFI document costs one windowed fetch per 100,000 characters. Tomo II has 485,126 characters; offsets 0-100,000 (earlier round) and 100,000-200,000 (this round) are read, leaving 200,000-485,126, i.e. three fetches.

Qatar's whole current and recent senior line is now read and every outside employer in it is public. The Peninsula's Who's Who profile of the previous governor (https://s.thepeninsula.qa/article/24/09/2013/whos-who-governor-of-qatar-central-bank-h-e-sheikh-abdullah-bin-saud-al-thani) gives Sheikh Abdullah bin Saud Al Thani's full career: QCB from 1982, Deputy Governor 1990-2001, Chairman of the State Audit Bureau 2001-2006, Governor from May 2006, and Chairman of Qatar Development Bank since its inception in 1996 - a state audit body and a state development bank, nothing private. The current board, as published in the Amiri appointment (https://www.qatar-tribune.com/article/189679/latest-news/amir-appoints-board-of-directors-of-qatar-central-bank/amp), is Governor Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saud Al Thani as chairman, Deputy Governor Sheikh Ahmed bin Khalid bin Sultan Al Thani as vice chairman, Dr Saleh bin Mohammed Al Nabit, Dr Tami bin Ahmed Al Binali and Dr Khalid Nasser Al Khater, plus unnamed undersecretaries of the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry: not one member is identified with a commercial bank, insurer or other private financial firm. The deputy governor's own appointment notices (https://s.thepeninsula.qa/article/12/02/2025/amir-appoints-deputy-governor-of-qatar-central-bank and https://www.gulf-times.com/article/700165/qatar/amir-appoints-qcb-deputy-governor) carry Decree No. 12 of 2025 and no career at all. The person refused in the earlier round was not re-opened.

The other side of the Qatar door was also tried and is closed on the bank-biography route. Qatar Islamic Bank's senior management page (https://www.qib.com.qa/en/senior-management/) publishes long careers for nine executives - Bassel Gamal (Commercial International Bank Egypt from 1990, Ahli United Bank Bahrain from 2001, Ahli Bank Qatar deputy CEO 2004-2006 then CEO to early 2009), Tarek Youssef Fawzi, Dorai Anand (Citibank 12 years, Al Rajhi Bank 8 years), Constantinos Constantinides, Khalefa Al Mesalam (HSBC Qatar, Commercial Bank of Qatar, Al Khaliji), Rakesh Sanghvi, Gourang Hemani, Saleem Ul Haq - and not one of them has ever worked at Qatar Central Bank, so none is a revolving-door move. Al Rayan Bank's director page for Omar Al Emadi (https://www.alrayanbank.co.uk/investor-relations-omar-al-emadi) gives AlRayan Bank QPSC from 2021, Al Khaliji Commercial Bank and Commercial Bank of Qatar before that, and again no central bank post. Qatar's banks publish fuller careers than QCB does, but the careers they publish do not pass through QCB.

Both Mauritanian career documents that name people were read and neither names a private financial employer. Financial Afrik's report of the 2014 deputy-governor appointment (https://www.financialafrik.com/2014/01/08/mauritanie-un-nouveau-gouverneur-adjoint-a-la-bcm/) names Cheikh Kebir Ould Moulaye Taher and describes his prior career only as 'ancien ministre', with no ministry, no dates and no employer; it mentions Generale de Banque de Mauritanie, which it calls the country's main business bank, only as the subject of a dispute with the monetary authorities, not as his employer, so there is no move to file. Financial Afrik's report on the 2020 reorganisation of the BCM organigramme (https://www.financialafrik.com/2020/09/29/mauritanie-la-banque-centrale-etoffe-son-organigramme/) names eight new directors and senior advisers - Dioulou Camara, Mohamed Ould Sidaty, Soko Ibrahim Bocar, Mohamed Lemine El Hadj Sidi, Cheikhna Bedad, Mohamed Abdallahi Mohamed, Lemina mint Sidi Baba, Bouna Kerkoub - and gives a prior employer for none of them beyond internal BCM posts and, for one, 'conseiller en informatique'.

The Mauritanian route most likely to convert was identified and not opened: the board and management pages of the country's own private banks, several of which are named in the search results as having publicly announced their leadership - Attijari Bank Mauritanie (Mohamed Boubrik named director general in 2019, Othmane Boudhimi in 2014), Banque Internationale d'Investissement / ex Societe Generale Mauritanie (Nicolas Roca), Banque Islamique de Mauritanie, Generale de Banque de Mauritanie, Banque El Amana. The next fetch here is one of those banks' own 'conseil d'administration' or 'gouvernance' page, searched with the French career phrase 'ancien directeur a la Banque Centrale de Mauritanie', because a Mauritanian private bank's own page is where both the career and the shareholder family would be stated in one document.

The two sitting deputy governors are read and both are lifetime central bankers. Matangi Tonga's report of their appointment by the Reserve Bank Board on 21 July 2023 (https://matangitonga.to/print/32748) gives 'Ungatea Latu, Deputy Governor Policy, as having 'served the bank for over 25 years' with a two-year secondment as adviser to the IMF South East Asia Group executive director, and Lata Tangimana, Deputy Governor Operations, as having 'also served the Bank for over 25 years' in general operations. Neither bio names ANZ, Bank of South Pacific, MBf, Westpac or any other private financial firm. With the two existing records (Tatafu Moeaki, Joyce Mafi) being ministry-and-multilateral careers, the governor and deputy-governor line of the National Reserve Bank of Tonga is now exhausted.

The non-executive directors of the National Reserve Bank of Tonga board were not reached - no board-profile page or annual-report governance section was opened this round. That is the remaining Tongan seam and the brief's own advice points at it: the next fetch is the NRBT annual report's board-of-directors section (reservebank.to publishes the annual reports as PDFs, so it can be downloaded and grepped rather than windowed), looking for a director identified with Bank of South Pacific, ANZ, MBf Bank or a private insurer. Ownership would then still have to be settled separately, most plausibly by BSP Financial Group's Port Moresby stock-exchange listing.

The full Banco Central de Timor-Leste board is now identified and the bank publishes no biography for any of them. The board page (https://bancocentral.tl/about/boarddir/) loads its content client-side, so WebFetch returned navigation only; downloading the raw HTML and extracting it gives the complete membership - Helder Lopes (Governor, chairman), Rafael Borges (Deputy Governor), Sara Lobo Brites (Deputy Governor), and board members Aicha Binti Umar Bassarewan, Benjamin de Araujo e Corte Real, Laurentina Domingas Barreto Soares and Joao Mariano de S. Saldanha - under a heading whose placeholder text still reads 'Add board members here.' There is a name, a title and a photograph for each and not one line of career. So the central bank's own pages cannot convert Timor-Leste, and the existing record (Helder Lopes, ministry and Asian Development Bank) remains the only career the bank's site supports.

Two Timorese routes left unopened. First, the deputy governors Rafael Borges and Sara Lobo Brites by name - a search on 'Rafael Borges' with the bank's name returned only the bank's own pages and unrelated Borges entries, so the next step is the Timor-Leste government's own 'tomada de posse' (swearing-in) releases on timor-leste.gov.tl, which carry a CV paragraph for each appointee; one such release for the governor is already indexed (https://timor-leste.gov.tl/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/Tomada-de-Posse-do-Governador-do-Banco-Central-de-Timor-Leste_PT_13.09.20231.pdf). Second, the commercial side: BNCTL (bnctl.tl/en/about) is state-owned and therefore cannot convert, which leaves the privately owned banks licensed in Timor-Leste - the Australian and Indonesian banks' local branches - whose own board pages would have to supply both a BCTL career and the ownership statement.

Sao Tome and Principe was searched but no Sao Tomean document was opened, so the country has not actually been tested this round and the budget ran out first. Three live paths were located and all three are unopened: (1) the central bank's own site publishes PDFs on bcstp.st, including Plano_Estrategico_2026_2030.pdf and a governor's speech (DISCURSO_DO_GOVERNADOR_DO_BCSTP.pdf) - the strategic plans are the kind of document that carries a governance section; (2) the Assembleia Nacional's own diaries, mirrored by the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies at www2.camara.leg.br/saotomeeprincipe (DAN20-IIS.pdf and DAN21-IIS.pdf were returned by search), which record the parliamentary hearings on central bank appointments and typically read out the appointee's career; (3) the 2022 dismissal of the previous governor, covered by Forbes Africa Lusofona, whose articles on the exoneration would normally recite the predecessor's career. The employer that would have to be settled either way is BISTP, Banco Internacional de Sao Tome e Principe, whose shareholding is split between the Sao Tomean state and Caixa Geral de Depositos, both public - so a Sao Tomean conversion probably needs Afriland First Bank STP or Ecobank STP instead, and their ownership would have to be stated by the group's own structure page.

Cuba looks structurally closed on this row rather than merely unsearched, and the reason should be recorded so the next round does not pay for it again. The existing record (Joaquin Alonso Vazquez, Banco Popular de Ahorro and CADECA S.A.) is already a state savings bank and the state currency-exchange entity. A search in Spanish for Banco Central de Cuba vice-presidents' careers returned only news coverage - a vice-president calling the cash shortage critical, the removal of an earlier president, the appointment of the current one, and a report that Cuba has authorised the formation of a corporate bank with foreign capital - and no career list for any official. Every bank a Cuban official can have worked in (Banco Popular de Ahorro, Banco de Credito y Comercio, Banco Metropolitano, Banco Financiero Internacional, Banco Exterior de Cuba, CADECA) is state-owned, which is why the country's only record is public and why an ownership fetch cannot help here. If Cuba is ever to convert it will be through the newly authorised foreign-capital corporate bank, or through a Cuban official's posting to one of the state's foreign joint-venture banks where the foreign partner's private shareholding is stated - neither of which was reachable in this budget.

checked_not_in_assignment.note: No country outside the seven assigned (BOL CUB MRT QAT STP TLS TON) was researched or filed. Candidates that came to mind while reading Qatari and Mauritanian bank pages - notably Bahrain and Morocco, whose banks' board biographies turned up in the same search results - were deliberately not followed, since neither is in this assignment.

leads_not_opened: BOL: ASFI Libro_Historia_Tomo_II.pdf offsets 200,000-485,126 (three WebFetch windows; curl is 404-blocked on the whole asfi.gob.bo host, so WebFetch is the only way in).
BOL: ASFI's current registers of banks and of insurers, for Banco de Cochabamba S.A. and Compania Boliviana de Seguros S.A. - the fetch that would settle both at once.
BOL: ASFI MEMORIA 1998 and 1999 (both indexed), which carry the SBEF-era tables categorising entities as 'bancos privados nacionales' and may still list the two 1994-liquidated banks.

BOL: the Los Tiempos insurance-day supplement (https://www.lostiempos.com/sites/default/files/edicion_online/especial_dia_mundial_del_seguro.pdf), a trade history of Bolivian insurers that may state Compania Boliviana de Seguros' shareholding; would be a weak source.

MRT: Attijari Bank Mauritanie, Banque Internationale d'Investissement, Generale de Banque de Mauritanie and Banque Islamique de Mauritanie - each bank's own conseil d'administration page, searched with 'ancien directeur a la Banque Centrale de Mauritanie'.
TON: the National Reserve Bank of Tonga annual report's board-of-directors section, for a non-executive director from Bank of South Pacific, ANZ or MBf.
TLS: timor-leste.gov.tl 'tomada de posse' releases for deputy governors Rafael Borges and Sara Lobo Brites, which carry CV paragraphs.

STP: bcstp.st's own PDFs (Plano_Estrategico_2026_2030.pdf), the Assembleia Nacional diaries mirrored at www2.camara.leg.br/saotomeeprincipe, and Afriland First Bank's group structure page for the ownership half.
CUB: the foreign-capital corporate bank Cuba has authorised (reported by OnCuba), the only route by which a Cuban official could reach a stated-private employer.
